title: What is Apache Pulsar — a distributed messaging system that combines Kafka-like durable log (BookKeeper storage) with RabbitMQ-like queue features (shared subscriptions, per-message ack) + multi-tenancy + geo-replication built-in — and when would you consider Pulsar over Kafka (multi-tenancy, simpler geo-replication, combined queue + streaming in one system)?
shortTitle: What is Apache Pulsar, and when would you consider Pulsar over Kafka?
topicTitle: Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS vs Pulsar

s1_definition.profdef: Apache Pulsar is a distributed messaging and streaming platform that combines a Kafka-like durable, append-only log with RabbitMQ-like queue semantics in a single system. Its storage and serving are separated: brokers are stateless and serve traffic, while Apache BookKeeper provides the durable, replicated log storage. Pulsar natively supports multiple subscription types including exclusive, failover, shared, and key-shared, giving both streaming fan-out and work-queue distribution with per-message acknowledgement. It also ships with first-class multi-tenancy through tenants and namespaces and with built-in geo-replication across clusters.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India wants one messaging platform that behaves like a permanent ledger when needed and like a shared work queue when needed, and that can safely host many independent departments on the same infrastructure. Kafka is great as the ledger but its work-queue behaviour and tenant isolation need extra effort. RabbitMQ is great as the work queue but is not the durable replayable ledger. Pulsar is the single platform that tries to be both: the ledger lives in a dedicated vault service (BookKeeper), the clerks at the counter (brokers) are interchangeable because they hold no state, each department gets its own walled area (tenant and namespace), and the same message can be either replayed like a log or shared out like a queue depending on how you subscribe.
s1_definition.oneliner: Pulsar is a log and a queue in one system, with stateless brokers over BookKeeper storage, native multi-tenancy, and built-in geo-replication.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Apache Pulsar is a distributed messaging and streaming platform that combines a Kafka-like durable, append-only log with RabbitMQ-like queue semantics in a single system. Its storage and serving are separated: brokers are stateless and serve traffic, while Apache BookKeeper provides the durable, replicated log storage. Pulsar natively supports multiple subscription types including exclusive, failover, shared, and key-shared, giving both streaming fan-out and work-queue distribution with per-message acknowledgement. It also ships with first-class multi-tenancy through tenants and namespaces and with built-in geo-replication across clusters.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India wants one messaging platform that behaves like a permanent ledger when needed and like a shared work queue when needed, and that can safely host many independent departments on the same infrastructure. Kafka is great as the ledger but its work-queue behaviour and tenant isolation need extra effort. RabbitMQ is great as the work queue but is not the durable replayable ledger. Pulsar is the single platform that tries to be both: the ledger lives in a dedicated vault service (BookKeeper), the clerks at the counter (brokers) are interchangeable because they hold no state, each department gets its own walled area (tenant and namespace), and the same message can be either replayed like a log or shared out like a queue depending on how you subscribe.

**One line to remember:** Pulsar is a log and a queue in one system, with stateless brokers over BookKeeper storage, native multi-tenancy, and built-in geo-replication.

sections.s2_technical:
Pulsar's first distinguishing idea is the separation of compute and storage. In Kafka a broker both serves clients and owns the partition data on its local disk, so adding capacity or recovering from a failed broker involves moving large amounts of partition data. In Pulsar the broker is stateless: it serves produce and consume traffic but the actual durable data lives in BookKeeper, a separate distributed log store made of nodes called bookies. A topic's data is a sequence of ledgers striped and replicated across bookies. Because brokers hold no data, you can add or restart a broker quickly and it simply picks up serving topics; scaling storage and scaling serving are independent decisions. This is powerful operationally but means you run and tune two systems, BookKeeper and the brokers, plus ZooKeeper or an equivalent for metadata.

Pulsar's second distinguishing idea is unified messaging through subscription types. A subscription is how consumers attach to a topic, and the type decides the delivery semantics. Exclusive means one consumer only. Failover means one active consumer with hot standbys. Shared means messages are distributed round-robin across many consumers like a classic work queue, with per-message acknowledgement so individual messages can be acked or redelivered independently, which Kafka does not do natively because Kafka tracks a single offset per partition per group. Key-shared means messages with the same key always go to the same consumer, preserving per-key order while still sharing load. For example, a settlement worker pool can subscribe in shared mode to pull trades one at a time and ack each as it finishes, while an audit consumer subscribes exclusively and reads the whole stream in order. This gives you RabbitMQ-style queues and Kafka-style streaming from the same topic.

Pulsar's third distinguishing idea is first-class multi-tenancy. The hierarchy is tenant, then namespace, then topic. A tenant is an isolated organisational unit, a namespace groups topics and carries policies such as retention, quotas, backlog limits, and access control, and topics live inside namespaces. This lets many teams share one Pulsar cluster with real isolation and per-namespace policy, whereas in Kafka multi-tenancy is achieved more loosely with naming conventions, ACLs, and quotas rather than a built-in tenant model.

Pulsar's fourth distinguishing idea is built-in geo-replication. You can configure a namespace to replicate across multiple clusters in different regions, and Pulsar handles asynchronous cross-region replication natively. In Kafka cross-region replication is typically done with separate tooling such as MirrorMaker 2 or a commercial replicator, which is capable but is an additional component to operate.

So when would you consider Pulsar over Kafka? Consider Pulsar when you need strong multi-tenancy because many independent teams or clients must share one platform with isolation and per-namespace policy. Consider it when you want simpler built-in geo-replication across regions without bolting on separate tooling. Consider it when you genuinely need both queue semantics (shared, per-message ack, work distribution) and streaming semantics (ordered replayable log) in one system, so you do not run both RabbitMQ and Kafka. Consider it when independent scaling of storage and serving, via the stateless-broker and BookKeeper split, is operationally attractive.

The senior nuance is the honest trade-off. Kafka has a far larger ecosystem, more mature tooling, Kafka Streams and ksqlDB, broad client and connector support, and more widely available operational expertise. Pulsar's architecture is elegant but has more moving parts (brokers, bookies, metadata store), so it can be more complex to run well. The decision should weigh Pulsar's native multi-tenancy, unified queue-plus-stream model, and built-in geo-replication against Kafka's ecosystem maturity and operational familiarity.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India is consolidating messaging platforms and evaluating Pulsar.

Problem 1 — Today the settlement team runs RabbitMQ for its work queue (distribute trades one by one to a worker pool, ack each when done) and separately runs Kafka for the durable, replayable event log for compliance. Operating two platforms is costly. This is exactly where Pulsar's unified model helps: one topic can be consumed in shared mode as a work queue with per-message ack and simultaneously in exclusive mode as an ordered replayable stream.

Problem 2 — Several independent departments (retail payments, trading, cards) must share one messaging platform but must be isolated so one noisy department cannot affect another's quotas or data. This is exactly what Pulsar's tenant and namespace multi-tenancy provides, with per-namespace retention and quota policy.

Problem 3 — The bank runs in Mumbai and a disaster-recovery region, and transaction events must replicate across regions without bolting on separate tooling. This is exactly what Pulsar's built-in geo-replication provides at the namespace level.

The demo models a simplified Pulsar. A `PulsarTopic` stores an append-only log (BookKeeper-like) and supports attaching subscriptions of different types. A `Subscription` has a type (EXCLUSIVE, SHARED, KEY_SHARED) that decides how messages are dispatched to its consumers, with per-message ack for SHARED. A `Namespace` groups topics under a tenant and carries a retention policy, demonstrating multi-tenancy, and a `geoReplicateTo` method illustrates cross-cluster replication. The `main` method publishes trade events, consumes them as a shared work queue and as an exclusive ordered stream from the same topic, shows two tenants isolated in namespaces, and shows a namespace replicating to a DR cluster.

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  application:
    name: pulsar-eval-service
pulsar:
  service-url: pulsar://pulsar-broker:6650
  tenant: nbi
  namespaces:
    payments: { retention: 30d, backlog-quota: 10GB }
    trading:  { retention: 7y,  backlog-quota: 50GB }
  geo-replication:
    clusters: [ mumbai, dr-pune ]
```

##### 4f. Logging notes

Appends to the BookKeeper-like ledger are logged at `fine`, while subscription creation, dispatch, replay, and geo-replication are logged at `info`, so the unified queue-plus-stream behaviour and tenancy are visible without ledger noise.
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a trading namespace under tenant nbi with seven-year retention, three trade events T-1, T-2, T-3 in the trade.events topic.

Step 1: The trading namespace is created with seven-year retention. The topic trade.events is created under it. These are isolated by tenant and namespace from any other department.

Step 2: Three trade events are appended to the topic's ledger, which is the BookKeeper-like durable log. Nothing is routed yet; the data is simply persisted and replicated in storage.

Step 3: A SHARED subscription named settle-workers is attached with two consumers, worker-A and worker-B. Dispatch distributes the three messages round-robin: T-1 to worker-A, T-2 to worker-B, T-3 to worker-A, and each message is acknowledged individually. This is classic work-queue behaviour from a log.

Step 4: An EXCLUSIVE subscription named audit is attached with a single consumer. Dispatch delivers all three messages in order to the one consumer. This is classic ordered streaming from the same topic that was just used as a queue.

Step 5: The audit subscription replays from the start, re-reading all three events in order, which is possible only because the data is a durable retained log rather than a consumed-and-gone queue.

Step 6: A second namespace, payments, is created under the same tenant with a different thirty-day retention policy, demonstrating that two departments share one platform with isolated policy.

Step 7: The trading namespace is geo-replicated to the dr-pune cluster, demonstrating built-in cross-region replication without extra tooling.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Apache Pulsar is a distributed messaging and streaming platform that combines a Kafka-like durable, append-only log with RabbitMQ-like queue semantics in one system. Its most distinctive architectural choice is the separation of compute and storage: brokers are stateless and serve produce and consume traffic, while the durable data lives in Apache BookKeeper, a separate replicated log store whose nodes are called bookies, with a metadata store such as ZooKeeper or etcd tying it together. Because brokers hold no data, you can scale and recover serving capacity quickly and independently of storage.

What makes Pulsar unified is its subscription types. A topic can be consumed as an exclusive or failover subscription, which gives a single ordered, replayable stream like Kafka, or as a shared subscription, which distributes messages round-robin across a pool of consumers with per-message acknowledgement like a classic work queue, or as a key-shared subscription, which keeps all messages of a given key on one consumer so you preserve per-key order while still sharing load. This means you get both queueing and streaming from the same topic, instead of running RabbitMQ and Kafka side by side. On top of this, Pulsar has first-class multi-tenancy through a tenant, namespace, and topic hierarchy with per-namespace retention, quota, and access policy, and it has built-in geo-replication that replicates a namespace across clusters in different regions natively.

You would consider Pulsar over Kafka in a few specific situations. You consider it when you need strong multi-tenancy because many independent teams or clients must share one platform with real isolation and per-namespace policy rather than Kafka's looser convention-and-ACL approach. You consider it when you want simpler built-in geo-replication across regions without bolting on separate tooling like MirrorMaker. You consider it when you genuinely need both queue semantics and streaming semantics in one system so you can retire a separate queue broker. And you consider it when independent scaling of storage and serving through the stateless-broker-over-BookKeeper design is operationally attractive.

At National Bank of India the evaluation was concrete. The settlement team was running a separate queue broker to hand trades one by one to a worker pool with per-message ack, and separately running a durable log for seven-year compliance replay, so Pulsar's ability to serve the same trade topic as a shared work queue and as an exclusive replayable stream was attractive for consolidation, while its tenant and namespace model let retail payments, trading, and cards share one cluster with isolated retention policies, and its built-in geo-replication covered the Mumbai-to-DR requirement. The honest senior caveat I always give is that Kafka still has the larger ecosystem, more mature tooling, Kafka Streams and ksqlDB, and more widely available operational expertise, whereas Pulsar's elegant architecture has more moving parts to run well, so the choice weighs Pulsar's native multi-tenancy, unified queue-plus-stream model, and geo-replication against Kafka's ecosystem maturity.

keyPoints: Kafka vs RabbitMQ: log-based vs message broker, persistence vs routing
Kafka vs SQS: self-managed vs managed, ordering vs simplicity
Kafka vs Pulsar: similar architecture, Pulsar has tiered storage
Choose based on: throughput, ordering, retention, operational complexity
